evidence: Quint. 1.7.10: cum sit c littera, quae ad omnēs vōcālēs vim suam perferat
terms.comment: A written sign for a sound; in the plural also a letter (epistle) and literature. A word ends in a letter, in a litterā terminātur, with the letter’s name in apposition, as the Romans put it (Traupman 238; Quint. 1.5.62 nōn e litterā, sed tis syllabā). Capitals are litterae grandēs and small letters minūtae (Plautus, Lewis & Short; Traupman 245).

phrases.latin: hoc eō nōn omīsī, quod quīdam eam, quotiēns a sequātur, necessāriam crēdunt, cum sit c littera, quae ad omnēs vōcālēs vim suam perferat
phrases.english: I mention this because some think it necessary whenever a follows, though c is a letter that carries its sound to all the vowels

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency (printed page numbers): p. 238, p. 245, p. 247.
Quintilian checked against the Perseus Latin texts, and cited by its numbering.
